instruction: Who is the person who keeps checking my arm with the bracelet on it?
response: That's your nurse! Nurses are really important helpers here at Children's Hospital. They check your bracelet — called an armband — to make sure you're getting exactly the right care and medicine meant just for you. It has your name, your birthday, and a special barcode on it. Your nurse will check it before giving you medicine, doing a test, or taking you somewhere in the hospital. Think of it like a library card, but instead of checking out books, it helps the hospital keep track of how to help YOU.

instruction: There's a lady who comes in and plays guitar and sings. Who is she?
response: She's a music therapist! Children's Hospital has a real music therapist who uses songs and instruments to help kids feel better. Music therapy can actually help with things like feeling less pain or being less worried. The cool part is you don't need to know how to play any instruments or be a good singer to join in — anyone can take part. If you liked her visit, you can ask your nurse if the music therapist can come back again!

instruction: Why does the doctor have other people following them around?
response: Great question! Those people might be medical students or residents. Medical students are grown-ups who are still in school learning how to become doctors. Residents have already finished medical school and are now practising to get even better at a special kind of medicine. They all work together as a team to take care of you, and the main doctor — called the attending physician — is in charge and makes sure everyone is doing a great job.

instruction: Who is the funny person with the red nose?
response: That's Ollie! Ollie is a therapeutic clown here at Children's Hospital. A therapeutic clown is someone specially trained to make kids laugh, play, and have fun while they're in the hospital. Ollie's whole job is to help your day feel a little more normal and a lot more silly. If Ollie made you smile, that means the clown magic is working!

instruction: Someone came and helped me do art. Is she a teacher?
response: She's kind of like a teacher, but her special job title is art therapist! The art therapy program at Children's Hospital lets kids like you draw, paint, and create things to help express how you're feeling. Sometimes it's easier to show your feelings through a picture than with words, right? Art therapy can help you feel more relaxed and in control, even when hospital stuff feels unpredictable. You can ask your nurse if the art therapist can visit again.

instruction: Who is the person who brought me food on a tray?
response: That person works with Patient Food Services! Their job is to bring meals to kids who are staying in the hospital. The kitchen team makes your breakfast, lunch, and dinner, and they bring it right to you. Breakfast usually comes around quarter to 8 in the morning, lunch comes before 1 in the afternoon, and dinner comes around 5 in the evening. If you're on a special diet, the food team works with your doctor and nurse to make sure you get exactly the right food.

instruction: There's a person who keeps asking me to move my arms and legs. Who are they?
response: That's probably a physiotherapist! A physiotherapist is someone who knows all about how your body moves. They might ask you to stretch, walk, or do little exercises to help your body get stronger or feel better. They're kind of like a coach for your muscles and bones. Everything they ask you to do is to help your body heal, even if it seems a little silly sometimes!

instruction: Who is the person who talked to my mom about how she's feeling?
response: That was probably a social worker. Social workers at Children's Hospital are here to help your whole family — not just you! They talk to moms, dads, and other family members about how they're feeling, and they can help with things like finding places to stay, figuring out tricky paperwork, or just being someone to talk to when things feel hard. It's their job to make sure your family is okay too.

instruction: A person let me play with a dog today! Who brought the dog?
response: How exciting! That was a therapy dog visit. Children's Hospital works with a group called St. John Ambulance to bring specially trained therapy dogs to visit kids. These dogs are super gentle and friendly, and spending time with them can make you feel happier and less worried. The person with the dog is a trained handler who makes sure the dog is safe and well-behaved. You can ask your care team if there's another therapy dog visit coming up!

instruction: Who is the person at the front desk when we walked in?
response: That person is a volunteer or an information desk helper! At Children's Hospital, there are friendly volunteers near the entrances — like at the B1 entrance and the B2 lobby — who help people find their way around the hospital. They can tell you which floor to go to, help you read a map, or point you in the right direction. Think of them as the hospital's welcome team! They're there from 8 in the morning to 3 in the afternoon on weekdays.

instruction: Someone came and talked to me about breathing and relaxation. Who was that?
response: That sounds like someone from the Heroes' Circle program! The Heroes' Circle visits kids at Children's Hospital every week and teaches really cool things like breathing exercises, relaxation tricks, and even some martial arts moves. These things can help you feel calmer and braver, especially when hospital stuff feels scary. If you liked it, you can ask your nurse about joining in next time they visit!

instruction: Who is the person who helped me practise talking?
response: That's a speech therapist! Speech therapists are part of your care team here at Children's Hospital. They help kids with things like talking, swallowing, and making sounds. They know lots of fun games and exercises to help your mouth and voice work their best. If you have questions about what you're practising together, your speech therapist is happy to explain!

instruction: There was someone in my room wearing gloves and a gown. Are they sick?
response: No, they're not sick at all! Sometimes people at the hospital wear extra things like gloves, a gown, or a mask to keep germs from spreading around. It's kind of like wearing a raincoat to keep dry in the rain — except this keeps germs away. It's actually a really smart way to keep you AND them healthy. Your nurse or doctor can explain why someone might need to wear that extra gear when they visit you.

instruction: Who is the person with the name tag who asked my name and birthday?
response: That could be any member of your care team — a nurse, a doctor, a therapist, or someone else helping to take care of you. They ask your name and birthday a lot, and that might seem kind of funny, but it's one of the most important ways they keep you safe! They check your armband and ask you these questions before giving medicine, doing tests, or taking you anywhere. It's like a secret password that makes sure everything is just right for YOU.

instruction: Someone gave my mom directions to a special room with toys. Who was that?
response: That might have been a Child Life Specialist, a volunteer, or your nurse! Children's Hospital has some really fun spaces. There's Ashley's Backyard on the sixth floor, which is a nature-themed playroom for younger kids. There's also a School-Age Activity Room with crafts, board games, puzzles, and LEGO. And there's even a SMILE Room with bubble columns, fibre optics, mirrors, and music! Your care team can help you find the play spaces that are open for you.

instruction: What's a Child Life Specialist?
response: A Child Life Specialist is one of the coolest people you'll meet at Children's Hospital! Their whole job is to help kids feel less scared and more comfortable. They might help you get ready for a procedure by explaining what will happen in a way that makes sense, or they might play games with you to help take your mind off things. They're also really good at helping you talk about your feelings. If you ever feel nervous or confused, a Child Life Specialist is a great person to talk to!

instruction: Who is the person who gave me medicine?
response: That was most likely your nurse. Nurses at Children's Hospital are the ones who give you your medicine and check on you throughout the day and night. Before they give you anything, they'll check your armband to make sure it's the right medicine for you. There are also pharmacists who work behind the scenes — they're the experts who prepare and check your medicine to make sure it's just right. If you ever have questions about your medicine, your nurse can get a pharmacist to come talk to you!

instruction: Why does one nurse leave and a new one shows up?
response: Great observation! Nurses take turns caring for you in something called shifts. One nurse takes care of you during the day, and then a different nurse takes over at night. When they switch — which happens around 7 in the morning and 7 in the evening — the two nurses talk right at your bedside to share everything about how you're doing. This is called a shift change report, and your mom, dad, or caregiver can listen in and ask questions too. That way, your new nurse knows everything about you!

instruction: There's a person who helped my mom fill out papers. Who are they?
response: That person might work at Patient Registration, or they could be someone from the Paediatric Family Resource Centre. Patient Registration is where families check in when they first arrive — it's on the second floor of Zone B. The Family Resource Centre on the first floor of Zone B also helps families with forms and paperwork. Both of these helpers are there to make the confusing stuff easier for your family!

instruction: Who is the security guard at the door?
response: That's a security guard, and their job is to keep everyone in the hospital safe — including you! At Children's Hospital, security guards are at the entrances, especially after 8:30 at night when the main doors are locked. They also walk around the hospital to check that everything is okay. If your family ever needs someone to walk them to their car or to the Ronald McDonald House, the security team can help with that too. They're like the hospital's protectors!

instruction: Somebody came and talked about what foods I can eat. Who was that?
response: That was probably a dietitian! A dietitian is a food expert who's part of your care team. They know all about which foods are best for your body, especially when you're in the hospital. They work with your doctor to make sure you're eating the right things to help you feel better. If you have allergies or there are foods you can't eat for religious reasons, the dietitian helps with that too. If you have questions about your meals, you can always ask!

instruction: Who's the person who helped me get dressed and do things with my hands?
response: That's an occupational therapist — OT for short! Occupational therapists help kids do everyday things like getting dressed, using their hands, and being more independent. They might give you fun activities or exercises that help your fingers, hands, and arms work better. They're like a coach who helps you get better at the things you do every single day!

instruction: I saw someone pushing a cart with cleaning stuff. Who is that?
response: That's a member of the housekeeping or environmental services team! Their job is super important — they keep the hospital clean and germ-free so that everyone stays as healthy as possible. They clean patient rooms, hallways, and all the spaces you use. Keeping things clean is one of the biggest ways the hospital stops germs from spreading. They're like the hospital's germ-fighting heroes!

instruction: Someone said they were a 'nurse practitioner.' Is that the same as a nurse?
response: That's a really smart question! A nurse practitioner is similar to a nurse, but they've done extra schooling so they can do some of the things doctors do too. At Children's Hospital, nurse practitioners work closely with the doctors to plan your care. Think of them as being right in between a nurse and a doctor — they're like a super-powered nurse who can help figure out what's going on with your body and decide on the best plan to help you feel better.

instruction: Who's the person who prayed with my grandma?
response: That was most likely a Spiritual Care Specialist. Children's Hospital has people whose job is to support families with prayer, quiet time, and spiritual comfort — no matter what you or your family believe. There's even a special room called the Sanctuary on the third floor of Zone C where anyone can go for quiet time, prayer, or just to sit peacefully. If your grandma or your family wants to talk to a Spiritual Care Specialist again, your nurse can contact one for you.

instruction: My nurse has a red bracelet on my wrist. Did she put it there?
response: Yes, your nurse or another member of your care team put that red bracelet on you. A red bracelet is a special allergy bracelet. It tells every single person who helps take care of you that you have an allergy they need to know about. It's like a little signal flag that says 'Hey, be careful with this!' That way, no one accidentally gives you something that might make you feel bad. It's there to keep you safe!

instruction: There's someone at the hospital who helped my dad find where to park. Who was that?
response: That was probably a volunteer or someone from the parking office! Children's Hospital has a parking garage called P8 off Baseline Road, and there are friendly people who help families figure out where to park, how to pay for their ticket, and how to get from the parking lot into the hospital. Guide volunteers near the entrances can also help with directions. Everyone works together to make sure families don't get lost!

instruction: What does a pharmacist do at the hospital?
response: A pharmacist is a medicine expert! At Children's Hospital, the pharmacy is on the first floor near the B1 entrance. Pharmacists make sure your medicine is exactly right — the right kind, the right amount, and safe for you. They also help your family understand how to give you medicine when you go home. If your family has questions about any medicine, your nurse can ask a pharmacist to come and explain everything. They're like the medicine detectives of the hospital!

instruction: Someone brought me beads and said I earn them. Who was that?
response: That was probably a Child Life Specialist telling you about the Bravery Beads program! Bravery Beads is a special program at Children's Hospital where each bead stands for something you've been through — like a test, a treatment, or a brave moment. Over time, you collect beads that tell YOUR story. It's totally up to you if you want to join — it's voluntary. But a lot of kids think it's really cool to see how many beads they earn. Each one is proof of how brave you are!

instruction: Who is the person who checked if my car seat was safe?
response: That was a Car Seat Technician! Children's Hospital has specially trained people who check car seats to make sure they're put in the right way. They can meet with your family in person or even do it over a video call. Making sure your car seat is installed properly is really important so you're super safe on the ride home. Your nurse can help your family set up a time to meet with a Car Seat Technician if you need one!

instruction: Why do nurses come check on me at night when I'm sleeping?
response: Your nurses check on you during the night because it's their job to make sure you're safe and comfortable — even while you're snoozing! They might look at a monitor, check your temperature, or just peek in to see that you're doing okay. It's kind of like how your mom or dad might check on you at night at home. Your nurse is always nearby, day and night, to help if you need anything.

instruction: Who is the person who let me use a laptop?
response: That was probably a Child Life Specialist! At Children's Hospital, Child Life Services has laptops that patients can borrow. There's even a cool website called Upopolis — it's a safe social network just for kids ages 8 to 18 who are in hospitals across Canada. You can connect with other kids going through similar stuff. If you want to use a laptop again, just ask a Child Life Specialist!

instruction: Someone told my mom about a house she can stay at near the hospital. Who was that?
response: That was probably a social worker or another member of your care team. They were most likely talking about the Ronald McDonald House! It's a special place near Children's Hospital where families who live far away from London can stay while their child is in the hospital. It's like a home away from home. If your family needs a place to stay, your care team can help figure out the best option.

instruction: There's a person who came with a translator for my family. Who set that up?
response: Someone on your care team arranged that! Children's Hospital offers free interpretation services, which means they can get someone to translate for your family so everyone can understand what the doctors and nurses are saying. It's really important that your family can communicate in a language they're comfortable with. If your family ever needs a translator again, just ask your nurse or anyone on your care team — they'll set it up.

instruction: Who is the person who helped me learn how to use crutches?
response: That was a physiotherapist! Physiotherapists are the experts at helping your body move safely. When you need crutches, a walker, or any other equipment to get around, they're the ones who teach you how to use it properly so you don't fall or hurt yourself. They'll practise with you until you feel confident. If something feels tricky or wobbly, tell your physiotherapist — they'll help you figure it out!

instruction: What's a resident? Someone said they were a resident.
response: A resident is a person who has already finished medical school — so they're a real doctor — but they're still learning and practising to become even better at one special kind of medicine. At Children's Hospital, residents work with the main doctor (called the attending physician) and help take care of you. They're like doctors in training who are getting really good at helping kids. Your main doctor is always keeping an eye on everything they do!

instruction: Who are the people wearing scrubs?
response: Lots of people at Children's Hospital wear scrubs — those are the comfy-looking pyjama-like outfits you see! Doctors, nurses, surgeons, and many other helpers wear them. Scrubs are worn because they're easy to keep clean, comfortable to work in all day, and they can be washed at very high temperatures to kill germs. So when you see someone in scrubs, it usually means they're someone who's here to help take care of patients like you!

instruction: Someone brought a machine to my bed and put stickers on my chest. Who was that?
response: That was probably a nurse or a technician. The stickers they put on your chest are called electrodes, and they connect to a machine that listens to how your heart is beating. It doesn't hurt at all — the stickers just sit on your skin. The person running the machine is specially trained to make sure everything looks good. If you have questions about what they're doing, it's always okay to ask them to explain!

instruction: Who are the people in the playroom?
response: The people helping out in the playroom could be Child Life Specialists or volunteers! Children's Hospital has some great play spaces, like the School-Age Activity Room on the sixth floor where you can do crafts, play board games, build with LEGO, and do puzzles. Child Life staff and volunteers plan fun activities and special events throughout the month. These helpers are there to make sure you have fun and feel more at home while you're in the hospital.

instruction: Someone said they're a 'unit clerk.' What's that?
response: A unit clerk is a helper who works at the nurses' station — that's the desk area where the nurses hang out when they're not in your room. The unit clerk helps with important behind-the-scenes stuff like answering the phone, organizing paperwork, and helping keep the unit running smoothly. They might not give you medicine or check your temperature, but without them, the whole floor would be a lot more confusing! They're an important part of the team.

instruction: Why did someone ask my mom if she wanted to talk to a lawyer?
response: That might have been a social worker telling your mom about a special program called Pro Bono Law Ontario. Children's Hospital has a partnership where families who need help with legal stuff — like paperwork, housing, or other problems that can affect your family — can talk to a lawyer for free. It doesn't mean anything is wrong! It's just another way the hospital tries to help families with things that might be stressful. Your mom can decide if she wants to use that help or not.

instruction: Who is the person who helped me when I was really scared before my surgery?
response: That was probably a Child Life Specialist! Their job is to help you feel less scared about things like surgery. They might have explained what would happen, let you see or touch some of the equipment, or taught you breathing tricks to calm down. At Children's Hospital, there's also a program where a parent can come with you into the operating room while you fall asleep — that's called the Parental Presence at Anaesthesia Induction program. Your care team wants you to feel as brave and calm as possible!

instruction: There was a person who talked to me about going home. Who was that?
response: That was someone from your care team helping you get ready for discharge — which is the word for going home from the hospital! It could have been your nurse, a doctor, or a social worker. They want to make sure your family knows everything about your medicines, any follow-up visits, and how to take care of you at home. Going home is exciting, and your care team wants to make sure you're completely ready!

instruction: Someone came and put cream on my arm before the needle. Who was that?
response: That was a nurse or another member of your care team using something called topical anesthetic — which is a special cream that numbs your skin so the needle doesn't hurt as much. It's part of something called the Comfort Promise at Children's Hospital. That's a promise the hospital makes to try to make needle pokes as pain-free as possible for every kid. They also have other tricks like distraction and comfortable sitting positions to help you feel better during needles.

instruction: Is the person who takes my blood a doctor?
response: Not always! The person who takes your blood might be a nurse, a lab technician, or sometimes a doctor. Lab technicians are people who are specially trained to draw blood and run tests on it. After they take a little bit of your blood, they send it to a lab where scientists look at it to help your doctor understand what's happening in your body. Whoever takes your blood, they'll check your armband first to make sure everything is matched to you!

instruction: Who's the person who took my picture with a big machine?
response: That was a medical imaging technician or technologist! They use special machines to take pictures of the inside of your body — like your bones, your tummy, or your head. It's kind of like a camera, but instead of taking a picture of your face, it takes a picture of what's going on inside you. These pictures help your doctor figure out the best way to help you. The technician is specially trained to use the machine and make sure you're comfortable.

instruction: Someone from the hospital showed up with toys when I was getting my needle. Why?
response: That was probably a Child Life Specialist or a nurse using a trick called distraction! It's part of Children's Hospital's Comfort Promise. When you're focused on something fun — like a toy, a video, or a game — your brain pays less attention to the needle. It's a real, proven way to make needle pokes feel less scary and less ouchy. Pretty clever, right? You can always ask for a distraction activity next time you need a needle.

instruction: Who is the person who makes sure my room is clean?
response: That's someone from the housekeeping team, also called environmental services. They come to your room to clean surfaces, take out trash, and make sure everything is tidy and germ-free. Keeping your room clean is one of the best ways to stop germs from spreading, and the hospital takes it very seriously. They might also ask your family to keep extra stuff to a minimum so they can clean every spot properly!

instruction: My nurse introduced me to a new nurse at her bedside. Why?
response: That's called a bedside shift change report! When one nurse's shift is ending and a new nurse is starting, they come to your bedside together to talk about how you're doing. They go over your care plan, do some safety checks, and make sure the new nurse knows everything important about you. Your parent or caregiver can listen in and even ask questions. It usually only takes about three to five minutes, and it helps make sure nothing important gets missed!

instruction: I saw a dog with a special vest in the hallway. Whose dog is that?
response: That's a therapy dog! The dog wears a special vest to show that it's working. Children's Hospital partners with St. John Ambulance to bring trained therapy dogs to visit kids. The handler — the person walking with the dog — makes sure the dog is gentle and safe. Therapy dogs can make you feel happier and less stressed. Family pets aren't allowed in the hospital, but therapy dogs are special because they're trained to visit patients. Ask your care team if a therapy dog visit is coming to your unit!

instruction: Who is the lady who talked to me and my siblings together?
response: That might have been a Child Life Specialist or a social worker. Both of these helpers work with your whole family — not just you. They know that when one kid is in the hospital, it can be tough for brothers and sisters too. They might have been talking to everyone about what's happening, answering questions, or just making sure your siblings feel included and okay. If any of you have more questions, you can always ask to talk to them again.

instruction: Why did someone come to my room with a computer on wheels?
response: That computer on wheels is called a WOW — a Workstation on Wheels! Nurses and other members of your care team use it to look up your information, enter notes about how you're doing, and check which medicines you need. It helps them keep all your important details right at their fingertips. It's kind of like how teachers have a laptop to keep track of everything — except this one rolls right to your bed!

instruction: I met someone who said they help with 'transitions.' What does that mean?
response: That person is part of the Transitions in Care team! They help kids and families through big changes — like going from being a kid patient to an adult patient when you get older, or going from the hospital back to school. Transitions can feel confusing, so having someone who guides you through it makes everything smoother. Think of them as a bridge between where you are now and where you're going next!

instruction: Someone in the hospital said they're a volunteer. What do volunteers do?
response: Volunteers are really kind people who come to Children's Hospital to help out without getting paid — they do it because they want to! You might see them at the information desks near the B1 entrance or B2 lobby, helping families find their way. Some volunteers help in playrooms, bring activity carts around, or help with special events. Guide volunteers are at the hospital from 8 in the morning to 3 in the afternoon on weekdays. They're some of the friendliest people you'll meet!

instruction: Why does my nurse keep washing her hands so much?
response: Your nurse is a germ-fighting superhero! Washing hands is the BEST way to stop germs from spreading in the hospital. Your nurse cleans their hands before coming into your room, when they leave, and lots of times in between. They usually use a special hand gel called alcohol-based hand rub. Everyone who visits you — family, friends, and helpers — should wash their hands too. It keeps you and everyone else in the hospital safe and healthy!

instruction: There's a room called the SMILE Room. Who takes me there?
response: A Child Life Specialist or your nurse can help you get to the SMILE Room! It's a really cool room on the sixth floor in room B6-261. It's filled with amazing things like bubble columns, fibre optics, mirrors, and music. It's designed to help you relax or feel more alert, depending on what you need. It's called the SMILE Room because it's hard not to smile when you're in there! Ask your care team if you can visit.

instruction: Who decides when I can go home?
response: Your doctor — called the attending physician — is the main person who decides when you're well enough to go home. But they don't decide alone! They talk to your nurses, and sometimes other people on your care team like a physiotherapist or social worker, to make sure you're truly ready. Your family is part of that conversation too. Your care team will give your family all the instructions you need before you leave so everything goes smoothly at home.

instruction: Someone talked to my mom about money stuff. Who was that?
response: That was probably a social worker. Social workers at Children's Hospital can help families figure out money things — like finding financial help, filling out applications for support, or understanding hospital bills. The hospital also has a Business Office in Zone D on the third floor if your family has questions about charges for things not covered by OHIP, like certain supplies. Your care team wants to make sure your family isn't stressed about money on top of everything else.

instruction: Who is the person who helped my mom stay with me overnight?
response: That was your nurse or another member of your care team! At Children's Hospital, they know how important it is for families to be together. Most patient rooms have a spot for a parent or caregiver to sleep — like a fold-out chair or a special sleep space with clean sheets, pillows, and blankets. Your nurse helps set that up and lets your parent know the rules, like staying in the room between 8 at night and 8 in the morning. Your parent can be right there beside you!

instruction: I saw someone with a pager clipped to their clothes. Who uses pagers?
response: Lots of people at Children's Hospital still use pagers! Doctors, Spiritual Care Specialists, and other team members carry them so they can be reached quickly anywhere in the hospital. A pager is like a tiny phone that just gets short messages. When someone needs a particular helper fast, they send a page, and that person knows to come right away. It's one of the ways the hospital makes sure help is never far away!

instruction: Someone asked me to blow into a tube. Who was that person?
response: That was probably a respiratory therapist or a nurse doing a breathing test! Respiratory therapists are experts on lungs and breathing. Blowing into a tube helps them learn how well your lungs are working. It might feel silly, but the information from that puff of air tells your care team a lot! If you're curious about what the results mean, your care team can explain it in a way that makes sense to you.

instruction: My mom talked to someone about going back to school. Who was that?
response: That was probably someone from the Transitions in Care team or a social worker. They help figure out how to make going back to school easier after a hospital stay. They might talk to your mom about what to tell your teacher, how to handle homework you've missed, or whether the school needs to know about any health stuff. It's their job to help make sure school feels smooth and normal again when you're ready to go back!

instruction: There's a special room where my mom pumps milk for my baby sibling. Who told her about it?
response: Your nurse or another care team member let her know! Children's Hospital has a breast pump room on the sixth floor in Zone B, room B6-235. The nurse gives moms special containers and labels for the breast milk, and then keeps it in the fridge or freezer for the baby. Moms can also buy breast pump kits from the pharmacy on the first floor near the B1 entrance. Everyone wants to make sure your baby sibling gets fed!

instruction: Why are there so many different people taking care of me?
response: Because you deserve the best team! At Children's Hospital, lots of different helpers work together to take care of every part of you — not just the part that's sick or hurt. Your doctor looks at the big picture, your nurse takes care of you day and night, a dietitian makes sure your food is right, a physiotherapist helps your body move, and a Child Life Specialist helps you feel happy and brave. Everyone has their own superpower, and together they make one amazing team!

instruction: Someone from the hospital talked to my family about keeping our culture's traditions. Who was that?
response: That might have been a Spiritual Care Specialist, a social worker, or the Youth Indigenous Wellness Consultant if your family is Indigenous. Children's Hospital cares about your family's cultural customs and religious beliefs, and they want to make sure those are respected during your stay. There's also an Indigenous Healing Space in the hospital for First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous families. Your care team is always happy to talk about ways to honour your family's traditions.

instruction: Who is the person who put a secret code on the door for my mom?
response: That was most likely your nurse on the B6 inpatient unit! That floor is a locked unit, which means the door needs a special code to open. When you're admitted there, your nurse gives your parent or caregiver a confidential code — kind of like a secret password — so they can get in and out. It's locked to keep all the kids on that floor extra safe. Only the people who are supposed to be there know the code!

instruction: There was a person in the emergency room who checked if I had anything dangerous. Who was that?
response: That was a security guard! At the Emergency Department at Children's Hospital, everyone walks through a special system that checks for things that could be dangerous, like weapons. It's really quick — you don't have to stop or take anything out of your pockets. The security guard is there to help if the machine beeps. It's the same idea as airport security — it's there to make sure everyone inside is safe. The guards are friendly and happy to explain what's happening if you're curious.

instruction: Someone offered to walk my dad to his car at night. Who was that?
response: That was a security guard! At Children's Hospital, the security team can walk family members to their car or even to the Ronald McDonald House if it's dark outside or someone doesn't feel safe walking alone. All your dad needs to do is call the security dispatch number, and they'll send someone to help. It's one of the ways the hospital looks after your whole family, not just you!

instruction: Someone put numbing cream on my skin before a needle. Why would a nurse do that?
response: Because your nurse wants the needle to hurt as little as possible! At Children's Hospital, they have something called the Comfort Promise. That means they try their very best to make every needle less painful and less scary. The numbing cream is called a topical anesthetic, and it makes your skin feel sleepy so you barely feel the poke. Your nurse might also help you sit in a comfy position or use toys and videos to distract you. They really do care about your comfort!

instruction: Who answers the phone when my grandma calls the hospital?
response: When your grandma calls Children's Hospital, she'll first talk to the hospital operator — that's the person who answers the main phone number. The operator can connect her to the right place, like the floor you're staying on. Once the call gets to your unit, the unit clerk or your nurse can help. Your grandma will need to give your full name, and then she can ask to speak with your nurse. Sometimes it's hard to get through during shift changes — around 7 in the morning and 7 at night — so those aren't the best times to call!

instruction: There's someone at the hospital who talks about feelings. Is that okay to do?
response: Absolutely! Talking about feelings is one of the bravest things you can do. At Children's Hospital, there are people whose whole job is helping kids with their feelings — like psychologists, social workers, and Child Life Specialists. Psychologists can help you learn tricks for dealing with worry, sadness, or frustration. Social workers help your whole family cope. And Child Life Specialists use play and activities to help you express yourself. You never have to keep big feelings bottled up. Talking about them is always okay.

instruction: Who is the person who helped me learn to eat differently after my surgery?
response: That could have been a dietitian or a speech therapist. A dietitian helps figure out which foods are best for you after surgery, especially if your tummy or body needs something different for a while. A speech therapist might help if you're having trouble swallowing or eating safely. They both work together with your doctor and nurse to make sure you're eating in a way that helps your body heal. If eating feels tricky, tell your care team!

instruction: Why do some people wear masks in the hospital?
response: People wear masks at Children's Hospital to keep germs from spreading. Masks help protect you, other patients, and the staff. Some people wear masks all the time, and sometimes you might see people wearing extra things like gloves and gowns when they come into your room. If there's a special sign on your door, it might mean extra germ-fighting steps are needed. Hospital masks are available right at the entrance for anyone who needs one. It's one of the ways the hospital keeps everyone healthy!

instruction: Who set up the TV and helped me watch shows in my room?
response: Your nurse or a staff member helped you get set up! Children's Hospital has a patient entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free. If your family has accounts for streaming services, you can use those too. If you have any trouble getting the TV or entertainment to work, you can ask your nurse or stop by an information desk for help. Having shows to watch can make the time go by a lot faster!

instruction: There's a person who helps kids who speak different languages. Who is that?
response: That's an interpreter! Children's Hospital has free interpretation services so that every family can communicate with their care team in a language they're comfortable with. The interpreter translates what the doctors and nurses say so your family can understand everything about your care. If your family speaks a language other than English, or if someone is deaf or hard of hearing, your care team can arrange for an interpreter anytime. Just ask!

instruction: Someone came in and helped me play a game while the doctor was doing something. Why?
response: That person was using something called distraction — and it's part of the Comfort Promise at Children's Hospital! When you're focused on a fun game or activity, your brain doesn't pay as much attention to what the doctor is doing, which makes it feel less scary and less painful. The person helping you might have been a Child Life Specialist or a nurse. It's a trick that really works, and it's one of the ways the hospital keeps its promise to help you feel as comfortable as possible.

instruction: My dad talked to someone about staying at a special house nearby. What house?
response: Your dad was probably hearing about the Ronald McDonald House! It's a special place right near Children's Hospital where families who live far from London, Ontario, can stay while their kid is in the hospital. It feels more like a real home than a hotel. There's also a Ronald McDonald Family Room inside the hospital. Your care team can help your dad figure out if your family can stay there and how to get set up.

instruction: Who takes care of really tiny babies in the hospital?
response: Really tiny babies are taken care of by a special team in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit — the NICU! The NICU has nurses, doctors, and other helpers who are experts at caring for the tiniest patients. They know exactly how to keep small babies warm, fed, and growing. Parents can be close to their baby too — there are special chairs for skin-to-skin cuddles, called kangaroo care, and sleeper chairs for resting right beside the baby.

instruction: Who is the person who helped me when I was really sick and needed lots of machines?
response: That was the team in the Paediatric Critical Care Unit — the PCCU. When kids are very sick and need extra-close watching and lots of special equipment, they go to the PCCU where a team of specially trained doctors, nurses, and other helpers are there around the clock. There are even two sleep spaces right at your bedside so your family can stay close. The PCCU team is there for the sickest kids, and they work really hard to help you get better.

instruction: I saw someone wearing a badge that said 'student.' Are they learning about me?
response: Kind of! That person is a medical student — a grown-up who is going to school to learn how to become a doctor. Children's Hospital is a teaching hospital, which means students come here to learn. They might listen to your heart, ask questions, or watch while your doctor does something. They always have a real doctor supervising them, so you're always in safe hands. You're actually helping them learn how to take care of kids — which is pretty cool!

instruction: Someone asked me if I wanted to join a research study. What does that mean?
response: That person was probably a doctor or a researcher. A research study is when the hospital is trying to learn new things about how to help kids get better. They might ask your family if you'd like to be part of it, but you absolutely do NOT have to say yes. It's completely your choice, and if you say no, your care won't change at all. Your parents can read all about the study and take their time deciding. Nobody will be upset if the answer is no.

instruction: Why do different people ask me the same questions over and over?
response: It can feel annoying, right? But there's a really good reason! Each person on your care team needs to hear important things directly from you to make sure they have the right information. When they ask your name and birthday, it's to keep you safe. When different helpers ask how you're feeling, it's because they each take care of a different part of your health. Think of it like this: your nurse, your doctor, and your physiotherapist all need the information for different reasons — kind of like how your teachers at school each need to know different things about you!

instruction: Someone gave us a special form to say nice things about a nurse. What was that?
response: That was probably information about the Great Moments Recognition Program! It's a way for patients and families to say thank you to staff members who made their hospital stay better. If someone on your care team was really kind or helpful, your family can fill out a short form on the LHSC website to recognize them. That person will get a special letter and a little gift to know that your family appreciated them. It's a really nice way to say thanks!

instruction: There's someone who helps families who need extra help because of how the world treats them. Who is that?
response: That might be a Black Health Navigator. Children's Hospital has trained health-care workers called Black Health Navigators who help Black patients and families navigate the hospital. They make sure your family's voice is heard and that you get the care you need. They can explain your health-care options and go with you to meetings with your care team. If you'd like to connect with a Black Health Navigator, ask your care team or check out the hospital's website.

instruction: Someone talked to my parents about Indigenous healing. Who was that?
response: That was probably the Youth Indigenous Wellness Consultant! This person supports the mental health and cultural wellness of Indigenous kids at Children's Hospital. They help blend traditional ways of knowing with the care you get at the hospital. There's also a special Indigenous Healing Space in the hospital that's open to First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous families. If your family is interested, your care team can help you connect with them and visit the healing space.

instruction: Who is the person who talked about what I eat at the hospital cafeteria?
response: If someone was helping your family find food in the hospital, it might have been your nurse, a volunteer, or the person working at the Tim Hortons spot called 'On the Go' on the second floor of Zone B. That's the closest place to buy food, and it's open on weekdays from 6:30 in the morning to 8 at night. There are also vending machines near the elevators in Zone B on the first and third floors. Your care team can help you find the best food options!

instruction: Who is the person who put the tiny bracelet on my baby brother?
response: That was a nurse in the NICU or the unit where your baby brother is staying. Babies under one year old get a regular armband AND a small security alarm band. The alarm band helps keep tiny babies extra safe — it's like a little protector that makes sure your baby brother stays exactly where he's supposed to be. It's one of the special ways the hospital watches over the very littlest patients!

instruction: Someone came in and cleaned the table and door handles in my room. Why?
response: That was someone from the housekeeping or environmental services team, and what they're doing is super important! They clean things like tables, door handles, and bed rails because those are spots where germs love to hang out. By wiping everything down regularly, they help stop germs from moving from one person to another. It's one of the biggest ways the hospital keeps you and all the other patients healthy. Those cleaners are real germ-fighting champions!

instruction: What does a medical student do here?
response: A medical student is someone who already graduated from regular university and is now in medical school learning how to be a doctor. At Children's Hospital, medical students get to practise by helping take care of kids like you — but they always have a real doctor or resident watching over them. They might listen to your heart, ask you questions, or help with your care plan. You're actually teaching them while they're helping you — how cool is that?

instruction: Someone gave me a schedule of when a dog would visit. Who made that schedule?
response: The therapy dog visits at Children's Hospital are organized through a program with St. John Ambulance. Your care team or a Child Life Specialist probably shared that schedule with you. The visits are planned ahead of time so kids can look forward to them. If you want to know when the next visit is happening on your unit, just ask your nurse — they'll know if one is coming up!

instruction: Who is the person who helped my mom figure out how to give me medicine at home?
response: That was probably a pharmacist or your nurse. At Children's Hospital, the pharmacy is on the first floor near the B1 entrance and is open on weekdays. Before you go home, a pharmacist can make a medicine calendar for your family that shows exactly when to give each medicine and how much. Your nurse also goes over all the medicine instructions. If anything is confusing, your family can always ask the pharmacist to explain it again — that's what they're there for!

instruction: I met someone who talked about a garden with butterflies. Who showed me that?
response: Someone on your care team or a volunteer probably told you about Alex's Butterfly Garden! It's a beautiful outdoor garden in Zone D on the second floor. It was created in honour of babies and infants, and it has benches and a soothing water fountain. It's a peaceful place where families, kids, and staff can go to sit quietly and enjoy nature. If you'd like to visit, ask your nurse or use the MazeMap app to find it!

instruction: Someone showed me the MazeMap app on a phone. Who was that?
response: That could have been anyone on your care team — a nurse, a volunteer, or an information desk helper! MazeMap is an app that has a map of the whole Victoria Hospital and Children's Hospital inside it. It helps families find their way around the big building. You can also use the wayfinding kiosks around the hospital or scan a QR code on posters near the elevators. It's like a treasure map for finding your way around the hospital!

instruction: There was a person in the family lounge who set up a coffee hour. Who was that?
response: That was probably a Child Life Specialist, a social worker, or a volunteer! The Culliton Family Lounge on B6-110 is a space for families on the B6 inpatient unit to relax and hang out. Special events like family coffee hours happen there so parents and caregivers can meet each other, take a break, and feel a little less alone. It's a nice way for families going through similar things to connect. If your parent wants to go to the next one, your nurse can tell them when it is!

instruction: Someone gave me a phone to call home. Who did that?
response: That was your nurse or another staff member! Children's Hospital has patient telephones that you can use for free to make local and toll-free calls. They want you to be able to stay in touch with your family and friends. You're also welcome to use your own cell phone if you have one. Staying connected to people you love is really important, especially when you're in the hospital!

instruction: Who is the person who made sure I could reach stuff from my bed and didn't fall?
response: That was probably your nurse! Nurses do a special check called a falls assessment to figure out if you might be at risk of falling. They make sure your bed rails are up, that you have slip-proof socks or slippers, and that everything you need is within easy reach. They also remind you to ask for help before getting up on your own. It's all about keeping you safe while you're here!

instruction: What's a psychologist? Someone said they were one.
response: A psychologist is a person who is trained to help with feelings and thinking. At Children's Hospital, psychologists help kids and families deal with the tough parts of being sick or in the hospital. They can teach you tricks for handling worry, sadness, or frustration. They might also check how well you're learning and thinking if your medical condition affects those things. If you're ever feeling overwhelmed, a psychologist is a great person to talk to — and your nurse can help set up a visit.

instruction: Who is everyone on my care team?
response: Your care team is like a dream team of helpers! Here are some of the people you might meet: your doctor (they're in charge of the big plan), your nurses (they take care of you day and night), a pharmacist (the medicine expert), a dietitian (the food expert), a physiotherapist (helps your body move), an occupational therapist (helps with everyday activities), a speech therapist (helps with talking and swallowing), a social worker (helps your family), a Child Life Specialist (helps you cope and play), an art therapist, a music therapist, and a Spiritual Care Practitioner. Not everyone will work with you, but the ones you need will be there!

instruction: Who are all the different nurses and why are there different types?
response: There are two main types of nurses you might meet: Registered Nurses (RNs) and Registered Practical Nurses (RPNs). Both of them take great care of you — they give medicine, check on you, and make sure you're doing okay. RNs have a bit more schooling and can do some extra things. Then there are Nurse Practitioners, who have done even MORE school and can do some things that doctors do, like figuring out what might be making you sick. They all work together like a team of superheroes, each with a different level of power!

instruction: What does the doctor actually do compared to everyone else?
response: Your doctor — called the attending physician — is like the captain of the team. They look at the big picture of what's going on with your health, work with everyone else to make a plan, and make the final decisions about your care. They also supervise the residents and medical students. While nurses are with you the most and handle your day-to-day care, and other specialists help with specific things, your doctor is the one who puts all the puzzle pieces together.

instruction: What's a nurse practitioner? Are they as qualified as a doctor?
response: A nurse practitioner, or NP, is a highly qualified health-care provider — they're registered nurses who went on to complete advanced graduate-level education and training. At Children's Hospital, NPs partner with the medical team and work closely with attending physicians to plan patient care. They can assess patients, order tests, and make treatment decisions. While NPs and physicians have different training pathways, both bring serious expertise to your care. If you're being seen by an NP, you're in very capable hands.

instruction: Who's the attending physician and what's the hierarchy on my care team?
response: The attending physician is the senior doctor who oversees your care. They're ultimately responsible for all clinical decisions. Below them in the training hierarchy are residents — fully graduated medical school doctors doing specialty training — and then medical students, who are still in medical school and participate in care under supervision. Nurse practitioners also partner with the medical team and function similarly to residents in terms of care planning. Your attending leads this team, communicates the care plan to your family, and supervises everyone else's work.

instruction: Someone mentioned they're a resident. What exactly is a resident?
response: A resident is a doctor who has completed medical school and is now doing additional training in a specific specialty — like paediatrics, surgery, or critical care. Residency is a hands-on phase where they work directly with patients under the supervision of an attending physician. At Children's Hospital, residents help develop and carry out your care plan. They've earned their medical degree, so they do have real medical knowledge — they're just in the process of getting deeper expertise. Your attending physician oversees everything they do.

instruction: What's the difference between an RN and an RPN?
response: Both Registered Nurses (RNs) and Registered Practical Nurses (RPNs) provide direct patient care at Children's Hospital — things like administering medication, monitoring your condition, and coordinating your care. The main difference is in their education and scope of practice. RNs complete a four-year university degree and may manage more complex clinical situations, while RPNs complete a shorter diploma program and often work alongside RNs. Both are licensed, knowledgeable, and integral to your care team. The nursing team works closely with each other and with your physicians to make sure your needs are met.

instruction: I keep seeing different students on my care team. How much of my care are they actually involved in?
response: Children's Hospital is a teaching hospital connected to Western University, so you'll likely interact with medical students as part of your care. They participate in things like physical exams, history-taking, and care discussions, but always under the supervision of residents and attending physicians. No medical student makes independent decisions about your treatment. They're there to learn, and your care quality isn't compromised — if anything, teaching hospitals tend to have strong protocols and oversight. If you're ever uncomfortable with a student being involved, you have the right to say so.

instruction: What does a Child Life Specialist actually do for teenagers? I'm not a little kid.
response: Totally fair question. Child Life Specialists aren't just for young kids — they work with patients up to age 18. For teens, their role shifts from play-based support to things like procedural preparation, pain management strategies, coping techniques, and emotional support. They can help you understand what's going to happen during a procedure in a straightforward way, connect you with resources like Upopolis (a secure social network for hospitalized patients ages 8–18), and advocate for your preferences to the care team. They're also available if you just need someone to talk to who isn't your parent or your doctor.

instruction: Who is the social worker and why do they want to talk to me?
response: Social workers at Children's Hospital provide emotional support, advocacy, and practical help to both patients and families. They might want to talk to you for a number of reasons — to see how you're coping emotionally, to help with family communication, to assist with discharge planning, or to connect you with community resources. They can also help with things like financial support, navigating insurance, and school transitions. It's not because something is wrong — it's a standard part of holistic care. Whatever you share with them is treated with confidentiality and respect.

instruction: Someone mentioned a psychologist vs a social worker. What's the difference?
response: Both support your mental and emotional well-being, but their training and focus differ. Psychologists at Children's Hospital have specialized graduate-level training in clinical psychology. They do formal assessments — like evaluating your thinking and learning skills if a medical condition affects them — and provide structured therapeutic interventions like cognitive-behavioural therapy. Social workers focus more broadly on connecting you and your family with support systems, advocacy, financial resources, discharge planning, and community services. Think of the psychologist as more clinically focused on your mental health, while the social worker addresses the wider picture of how your family navigates the system.

instruction: What's the deal with the therapy dogs? How does that actually work?
response: Children's Hospital partners with St. John Ambulance to run a therapy dog program on several units. The dogs are specifically trained and certified for hospital environments — they're calm, gentle, and screened for health and temperament. Visits are scheduled by the program and the care team, and a trained handler always accompanies the dog. There's research showing that interaction with therapy animals can reduce stress, lower blood pressure, and improve mood. Family pets aren't allowed for infection control reasons, but these therapy dogs go through a rigorous vetting process. Ask your care team if a visit is coming up on your unit.

instruction: I heard there's a therapeutic clown. Isn't that kind of childish?
response: I get why that might seem that way. Ollie is a therapeutic clown at Children's Hospital, and while the approach is definitely geared more toward younger patients, the role is actually more nuanced than you'd think. Therapeutic clowns are trained professionals who use humour and play to help normalize the hospital environment. For teens, Ollie might not be your thing — and that's completely fine. Children's Hospital has plenty of other support options for older patients, like music therapy, art therapy, the Heroes' Circle program, and Upopolis. You get to choose what works for you.

instruction: Who are the people involved in the Comfort Promise?
response: The Comfort Promise is a hospital-wide commitment at Children's Hospital to minimize pain and anxiety during needle procedures. It involves multiple members of your care team. Your nurse will typically apply topical anesthetic to numb the skin before a needle stick. A Child Life Specialist might offer distraction techniques. Your care team will use comfort positioning — supportive body positions rather than restraint — to help you feel more in control. For infants, sucrose and breastfeeding are used. The philosophy is evidence-based: untreated procedural pain can lead to increased pain sensitivity, health-care avoidance, and even vaccine hesitancy. You're encouraged to advocate for yourself and ask about these options before any needle procedure.

instruction: Who's the music therapist and what can they actually do for me?
response: Children's Hospital has an accredited music therapist who uses music-based activities to support patients' health and well-being. It's not just background music — music therapy is a clinical intervention that can help with pain management, rehabilitation, emotional processing, and stress reduction. You don't need any musical skill to participate. Sessions are individualized and can range from listening to making music depending on what you're dealing with. It's available to patients of any age, illness, or disability. If you're interested, ask your nurse to set up a session.

instruction: What does the art therapist do? Is it just drawing?
response: It's more than that. The art therapy program at Children's Hospital provides kids and teens with a way to express thoughts and feelings through creative activities — and that can include drawing, but also painting, sculpting, collage, and other media. The point isn't to make great art; it's that the creative process itself can be empowering, relaxing, and therapeutic. Art therapy can give you a sense of personal control during a time when a lot feels unpredictable. For teens especially, it can be a way to process complex emotions that are hard to put into words.

instruction: Someone from security scanned me at the ER entrance. Why?
response: Children's Hospital has a weapons detection system at the Emergency Department entrance. Everyone entering the ED is required to pass through it — including patients, visitors, and even kids with a parent or guardian. The system uses non-invasive technology that lets you walk through without stopping or removing personal items. If something flags, a trained security guard may check your belongings. It's about maintaining a safe environment for patients and staff. There are accommodations available if someone can't go through the system in the standard way — you can speak with the security guard at the entrance about that.

instruction: Who should I reach out to if I want to give feedback about my care — good or bad?
response: There are a couple of options. For concerns or complaints, the first step is to talk directly to your care team. If that doesn't resolve things, you can contact the Patient Relations Office — they're reachable by phone at extension 52036 or by email at patientrelations@lhsc.on.ca. They check messages between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. on weekdays. If you want to recognize someone who made a difference, Children's Hospital has the Great Moments Recognition Program — you can fill out a short form on the LHSC website, and that person will receive a letter of appreciation. Your voice matters, whatever the feedback.

instruction: I'm trans. Is there anyone at this hospital who gets that?
response: Yes. Children's Hospital has the Gender Pathways Service, or GPS. It's a multidisciplinary service providing gender-affirming care to gender diverse and transgender children and adolescents 17 and under. The team follows North American and international guidelines, including those from the World Professional Association for Transgender Health. You can learn more or reach out to them directly at gps@lhsc.on.ca. If you want, your care team can also help connect you. You deserve to feel respected and understood during your care.

instruction: What does the dietitian actually do and why do they need to talk to me?
response: A dietitian at Children's Hospital is a nutrition expert who works with your medical team to ensure your diet supports your recovery and overall health. They might talk to you for several reasons — your medical condition may require a specific diet, you may have allergies or dietary restrictions that need to be managed, or they may need to adjust your nutrition plan post-surgery. LHSC offers a range of diets including vegan, vegetarian, Halal, Kosher, and allergen-specific options. If you have specific preferences or needs, the dietitian is the person to coordinate that. They're not there to lecture you — they're there to work with you.

instruction: Why does my nurse do a report at my bedside when the shifts change?
response: That's called a bedside shift change report, and it happens twice a day — typically around 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. The outgoing nurse and incoming nurse meet at your bedside to review your plan of care, complete safety checks, and make sure nothing falls through the cracks. You and your family are invited to participate — you can ask questions, share observations, or add information you think is important. It takes about three to five minutes. It's designed to keep communication transparent and to make sure your new nurse is fully up to speed on your situation.

instruction: What's a physiotherapist going to do for me?
response: A physiotherapist, or PT, focuses on your body's movement and physical function. At Children's Hospital, they might work with you on rehab exercises, mobility training, strengthening, pain management, or helping you safely use mobility aids like crutches or walkers. They assess where you are physically and create a plan to help you recover function or manage a condition. If you're post-surgical or dealing with an injury, your PT is key to your recovery. They'll explain the rationale behind what they're asking you to do, and you should feel free to ask questions.

instruction: What's an occupational therapist and how is that different from a physiotherapist?
response: While they overlap in some ways, occupational therapists (OTs) and physiotherapists (PTs) focus on different things. A PT works on movement, strength, and mobility — think walking, balance, and physical recovery. An OT focuses on your ability to perform daily activities — getting dressed, using your hands effectively, managing self-care tasks, and adapting to any limitations. At Children's Hospital, if your condition affects how you function in day-to-day life, an OT will work with you on strategies and tools to maximize your independence.

instruction: I've been asked about research. What should I know about the people running these studies?
response: Clinical research at LHSC is conducted by researchers and physicians, and every study must be reviewed and approved by the London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute (LHSCRI) and a qualified Research Ethics Board. Children's Hospital is also home to the Children's Health Research Institute (CHRI), which focuses specifically on child health. If you're approached about a study, you should receive a Letter of Information that explains everything — the purpose, risks, what's expected of you, and your rights. Participation is always voluntary, and declining won't affect your care in any way. Take your time reading the materials and ask as many questions as you need.

instruction: Someone mentioned a Black Health Navigator. What do they do?
response: Black Health Navigators are trained, registered health-care workers at LHSC who support Black patients and families in navigating the health-care system. Their role includes providing information about health-care options, ensuring your voice is heard in conversations with your care team, and advocating for equitable care. You can access this service through Black Health at the hospital — ask your care team or email BlackHealth@lhsc.on.ca. It's a resource designed to address specific systemic barriers that Black patients may face in health care.

instruction: What does the Youth Indigenous Wellness Consultant do?
response: The Youth Indigenous Wellness Consultant at Children's Hospital supports the mental health and cultural wellness of Indigenous children and youth accessing care at the hospital. Their approach bridges traditional Indigenous ways of knowing with Western medical approaches to healing. This service is available to all Indigenous kids — First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous. There's also an Indigenous Healing Space in the hospital that's open to Indigenous families with priority access. If you'd like to connect with the consultant, your care team can facilitate that, or you can reach Indigenous Health via email at IndigenousHealth@lhsc.on.ca.

instruction: What's a speech therapist actually for? I can talk fine.
response: That's a common misconception — speech therapists (also called speech-language pathologists) do way more than help with talking. At Children's Hospital, they also work on swallowing difficulties, voice disorders, language processing, and communication challenges that might result from a medical condition, surgery, or neurological issue. If you're seeing a speech therapist, it could be for any of those reasons. They're trained specialists who assess and treat a range of communication and swallowing needs.

instruction: Someone brought up spiritual care. I'm not religious — is that still relevant to me?
response: It can be. Spiritual Care at Children's Hospital is available to everyone regardless of religious background. Spiritual Care Specialists provide what the hospital calls 'people-centred care' — they work with patients and families on emotional support, coping, grief, meaning-making, and reflection. They're respectful of all beliefs, values, and practices, including having none. There's also a Sanctuary space in Zone C on the third floor that's open 24/7 for anyone who wants quiet time, reflection, or meditation. If you're dealing with heavy emotions during your stay, Spiritual Care can be a resource even if religion isn't part of the picture.

instruction: What's the point of the information desk volunteers?
response: The information desk volunteers and guide volunteers at Children's Hospital help patients and families navigate the building — which can be pretty confusing. Information desks are open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays and noon to 4 p.m. on weekends. Guide volunteers are stationed at the B1 entrance and B2 lobby from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. on weekdays. They can help you read room numbers (which follow a specific format like B2-503 — Zone B, Floor 2, Room 503), direct you to services, or just point you the right way. When you're stressed and in an unfamiliar building, having a friendly person who knows the layout can make a real difference.

instruction: What's the security team's role here? They're not just standing around, right?
response: Definitely not. Security at Children's Hospital has a pretty significant role. They control access to the building — the main B Tower entrance locks at 8:30 p.m. and caregivers need to check in with security after hours. They operate the weapons detection system at the Emergency Department. They patrol the hospital grounds. They can escort you or your family to the parking lot or Ronald McDonald House after dark. Certain zones and floors are locked 24/7, and security manages access to those areas. If there's an emergency, the Emergency Response extension is 55555. For non-emergencies, security dispatch is at extension 52281.

instruction: I noticed my care partner can only bring one other person. Who decides that?
response: The Care Partner Presence Policy at LHSC sets those limits. For inpatients, up to two care partners can be at the bedside at one time. For outpatients, it's one care partner per patient. The policy is monitored to align with provincial standards and infection prevention recommendations. During outbreaks or for patients with COVID precautions, only essential care partners are allowed. These aren't arbitrary rules — they're designed to balance family presence with patient safety and infection control. Your care team can provide more details about specific permissions and any exceptions.

instruction: What does the pharmacist do beyond just filling prescriptions?
response: At Children's Hospital, pharmacists are medication specialists who do a lot more than fill bottles. They review all your medications — prescription, over-the-counter, herbal, vitamins, creams, inhalers, everything — to check for interactions and appropriate dosing. They consult with your care team on medication choices. If you're on multiple medications, a pharmacist can prepare a medication calendar and review it with you and your family before discharge. They're available to answer questions about side effects, timing, and drug interactions. The pharmacy is located at B1-001, open Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. You can ask your nurse to have a pharmacist come to your room anytime.

instruction: My parents were told about a 'Decision Coach.' What is that?
response: A Decision Coach is part of LHSC's Shared Decision Making program. When you and your family face an important medical choice — like deciding between treatment options — a Decision Coach helps structure the process. They work with you, your caregivers, and your health-care providers to make sure you understand the evidence, weigh the risks and benefits, and factor in your personal values. It's about making informed decisions collaboratively rather than having something just decided for you. Your care team can refer you, or you can ask about it directly.

instruction: Who handles my personal health information and privacy?
response: Privacy at LHSC is taken seriously. Your personal health information (PHI) can only be shared with your parent(s) or legal guardian(s). You have the right to consent to or refuse collection, use, and disclosure of your PHI; to access your records; to be notified of inappropriate access; and to challenge the hospital's compliance with privacy laws. The Privacy Office can be reached at extension 32996 or privacy@lhsc.on.ca. If you have concerns about who's seeing your information, that's a conversation worth having with your care team. Your rights around your health information are protected by law.

instruction: Is there a lawyer I can talk to? My family is going through a lot.
response: Children's Hospital has a partnership with Pro Bono Law Ontario (PBLO) that provides free legal assistance to low-income families whose child is an inpatient or outpatient. It's a medical-legal partnership that recognizes legal problems — housing, benefits, custody, immigration — can directly affect a child's health and a family's ability to provide care. A social worker on your care team can refer you to the on-site triage lawyer. It's a legitimate resource that's there specifically for families in your situation.

instruction: What does the Transitions in Care team do for someone my age?
response: The Transitions in Care team at Children's Hospital supports patients and families through key transition points. For teens, two of the biggest ones are transitioning from paediatric to adult care as you age out of the children's system, and navigating the shift between school and hospital and back again. They help coordinate communication between your care team, your school, and your family so nothing gets lost in the gaps. If you're approaching 18 or have a chronic condition that will require ongoing adult care, this team is especially relevant — they help make sure the transition is planned rather than abrupt.

instruction: What's Upopolis and who runs it?
response: Upopolis is a free, secure social networking site for hospitalized paediatric patients ages 8 to 18. It lets you connect with other patients across Canadian hospitals who are going through similar experiences. It's managed through Child Life Services at Children's Hospital, and laptops are available to access it. If you're interested, talk to a Child Life Specialist — they can set you up. It's a way to feel less isolated during a hospital stay, especially if your friends at home can't fully relate to what you're dealing with.

instruction: What's Bravery Beads? Someone offered it to me but I feel like I'm too old for beads.
response: That's a fair reaction. Bravery Beads is a voluntary program at Children's Hospital designed for patients of all ages dealing with long-term or chronic illness or injury. Each bead represents a specific element of your care or treatment — procedures, milestones, challenges. For some patients, including teens, it becomes a tangible record of what they've been through. It's not really about the beads themselves — it's about documenting your journey. Some people find it meaningful, others don't, and both are completely valid. No pressure either way.

instruction: Someone at the hospital mentioned the Heroes' Circle. What is that?
response: The Heroes' Circle is a year-round program that provides weekly visits to both inpatients and clinic patients at Children's Hospital. It teaches breathing exercises, relaxation techniques, and martial arts. It's designed to help paediatric patients and their siblings manage stress, build confidence, and develop coping skills. It's not just for younger kids — the techniques are relevant for anyone dealing with medical challenges. If it sounds like something you'd want to try, ask your care team about the next session.

instruction: Who is involved in the PPI program?
response: PPI stands for Parental Presence at Anaesthesia Induction. The program involves your care team, a Child Life Specialist, and an anaesthesiologist. It offers an education session and potentially a tour of Day Surgery and the Operating Room to help you and one caregiver prepare for surgery. The program allows one caregiver to accompany you into the OR during the induction phase of anaesthesia — the part where you're falling asleep. Not every patient or caregiver is eligible, so discuss it with your care team or a Child Life Specialist if you're interested.

instruction: What does the unit clerk do and can I ask them questions?
response: The unit clerk works at the nurses' station and handles a lot of the administrative coordination on your unit — answering phones, processing orders, managing paperwork, and helping keep operations running smoothly. You can ask them general questions about the unit, like where something is located or when a visitor might be able to come, but clinical questions about your care should go to your nurse or doctor. They're approachable and can usually point you to the right person if they can't answer something directly.

instruction: My nurse said I should talk to someone about how I'm adjusting. Who did she mean?
response: She was likely referring to a paediatric psychologist or possibly a social worker. Psychologists at Children's Hospital provide assessment and treatment for patients experiencing challenges adjusting to illness, hospitalization, or disability.
