They teach coping strategies for managing physical, emotional, and behavioural symptoms. They can also assess cognitive and learning skills if your medical condition affects those areas. Social workers provide emotional support too, along with practical advocacy. Both are solid options depending on what you're dealing with — your nurse can help facilitate a referral.

instruction: What does the PCCU team look like and who will I see there?
response: The Paediatric Critical Care Unit (PCCU) is staffed by a specialized team trained to care for the most critically ill or injured children. You'll see intensivists (doctors who specialize in critical care), critical care nurses who provide very close monitoring, respiratory therapists, and potentially other specialists depending on your condition. The nurse-to-patient ratio is typically much lower than on a general unit, meaning your nurse is focused on fewer patients. Two family sleep spaces are available at the bedside, plus a quiet room and a sleep room nearby. The team communicates closely with families about what's happening, and you should feel empowered to ask questions.

instruction: Who works in the NICU and what do they do for the babies?
response: The Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) has a team of neonatologists (doctors specializing in newborn care), specially trained nurses, respiratory therapists, dietitians, and other specialists focused on critically ill or premature infants. They manage everything from breathing support and feeding to monitoring for complications. The NICU is a high-tech environment with a lot of equipment, but the team also prioritizes family-centred care — parents are encouraged to participate through skin-to-skin kangaroo care and bedside presence. There's a separate family guide for the NICU with more details if you have a sibling there.

instruction: Can I request a specific nurse or doctor?
response: You can express a preference, and your care team will do their best to accommodate it where possible. However, staffing assignments depend on factors like nurse-to-patient ratios, shift schedules, and unit needs, so there's no guarantee. If you have a specific reason for the request — like a strong rapport with a particular nurse or a communication issue with a team member — it's worth mentioning to the charge nurse or your care team. At the very least, they'll take your feedback seriously.

instruction: What does the Patient Relations Office actually do?
response: The Patient Relations Office at LHSC is the formal channel for questions, concerns, and feedback about care experiences. Their Patient Relations Specialists serve as a neutral point of contact between you and the hospital. They're reachable at extension 52036 or 58230, by email at patientrelations@lhsc.on.ca, or through an online contact form on the LHSC website. They check messages between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. on weekdays. They recommend starting with your care team first if you have a concern, but if that doesn't resolve things, they're the next step. You also have the option of submitting feedback in French.

instruction: Why does everyone keep checking my armband? It's getting annoying.
response: I get it — it can feel repetitive. But armband checks are one of the most critical safety protocols in the hospital. Before any medication, test, procedure, or transport, staff verify your identity by checking your armband — which has your name, date of birth, hospital ID, and a barcode. It's a standard practice designed to prevent medical errors, like giving the wrong medication or performing the wrong procedure on the wrong patient. These errors are rare precisely because of this kind of verification. If you have allergies, you'll also have a red bracelet that alerts every member of your care team.

instruction: There are interpreters here? How does that work?
response: LHSC offers free interpretation services for patients. If English isn't the language you're most comfortable with, or if you're deaf, deafened, or hard of hearing, you can request an interpreter through your care team. The hospital provides sign language and deaf-blind translation, relay services via the telephone company, and spoken language interpreters. There's a downloadable list of available spoken languages on the LHSC website. The goal is to make sure you can fully understand and participate in conversations about your care — and that your care team understands you. Don't hesitate to ask for this service.

instruction: Who's the Ontario Health atHome Care Coordinator and why did they talk to my family?
response: The Ontario Health atHome Care Coordinator helps patients and families plan for services and equipment that may be needed at home after discharge. If your hospital stay is longer than 14 days, a new referral to Ontario Health atHome is required. They assess your needs — things like home nursing support, medical equipment, or therapy services — and coordinate access to those community-based resources. If you're already receiving community services, you need to connect with the coordinator at extension 52249 before going home. They're essentially the bridge between hospital care and home care.

instruction: Who handles the food I get while I'm here?
response: Patient Food Services is responsible for your meals during your hospital stay. Your physician prescribes a diet based on your medical needs, and the food services team prepares meals accordingly. Breakfast is typically served between 7:45 and 8:45 a.m., lunch between 11:45 a.m. and 12:45 p.m., and dinner between 4:45 and 5:45 p.m. You'll get a form on your breakfast tray to select food for the next day. The hospital accommodates a range of dietary needs — vegan, vegetarian, Halal, Kosher, and allergen-specific diets. If you have concerns about your diet, talk to your care team or ask to speak with a dietitian.

instruction: My parents are stressed. Is there someone who can help them too?
response: Absolutely — and it's good that you're thinking about them. Social workers at Children's Hospital provide emotional support, advocacy, and practical information for families coping with a child's hospitalization. They can connect your parents with community resources, financial support, and counselling. There's also the Paediatric Family Resource Centre in B1-006 that offers peer support and help with forms and applications. A Spiritual Care Specialist is available via pager 14693 for emotional and spiritual support. Your parents can also access a quiet Sanctuary space on the third floor of Zone C anytime. Encourage them to talk to your care team about what they need.

instruction: What's PSMSC? Someone mentioned it.
response: PSMSC stands for Paediatric Symptom Management and Supportive Care Services. It's a specialized service at Children's Hospital for infants, children, and teens with serious illnesses, regardless of the underlying condition. Their goal is to alleviate all kinds of pain and suffering and support the best possible quality of life — including for children approaching end of life. PSMSC provides an additional layer of care on top of what your primary team is doing. If you or your family has been introduced to this team, it means the hospital is making sure all aspects of your comfort and well-being are being addressed.

instruction: Why did a nurse ask my parent to leave the room briefly?
response: There are a few reasons this might happen. Sometimes it's to provide care that requires clinical focus and space. Other times, it could be during mandatory safety checks or a procedure. In some cases, your care team may want to talk to you privately — this is standard practice with adolescent patients to give you the opportunity to share concerns or ask questions you might not feel comfortable raising in front of a parent. It's not unusual and it's not a sign of anything being wrong. Your parent is always welcome to come back right after.

instruction: What exactly happens during a shift change? I always notice a lot of activity around 7.
response: You're picking up on the nursing shift change, which happens at approximately 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. daily. During the transition period — roughly 6:45 to 7:30 — the outgoing and incoming nurses exchange information about each patient. At Children's Hospital, this includes a bedside shift change report where both nurses come to your room, review your care plan, complete safety checks, and invite you and your family to ask questions or share anything relevant. It's about a three to five minute process. Phone calls to the unit may be harder to get through during these windows, so it's best to avoid calling between 6:45 and 7:30 if possible.

instruction: Is there anyone who can help me deal with going back to school after this?
response: The Transitions in Care team and social workers at Children's Hospital can help with the school transition. They can coordinate communication with your school — speaking with your teacher, principal, or other staff about what you've been through, homework you've missed, accommodations you might need, and a return plan. Psychologists can also help if you're anxious about going back. It's worth bringing this up with your care team before discharge so everything is in place by the time you're ready to return.

instruction: Someone mentioned the Paediatric Family Resource Centre. What's there?
response: The Paediatric Family Resource Centre is in room B1-006 on the first floor of Zone B. It offers patients and families peer support, help with forms and applications, health information from a lived-experience perspective, and internet access. Hours are 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday; 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Tuesday and Thursday; and 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday by appointment only. It's also a quiet place to go when you need a break from your room. The people there have real-world experience navigating the system and can point you toward useful resources.

instruction: Can I have a say in my own care? It feels like everything is decided for me.
response: You absolutely can and should have a say. Children's Hospital sees families — including you — as partners in care. You're encouraged to ask questions, request explanations of any treatments, tests, or medications, and express your preferences. The Shared Decision Making program at LHSC exists specifically to ensure patients and caregivers collaborate with health-care providers on important choices. If you feel like your voice isn't being heard, tell your nurse, ask to speak with a social worker, or contact Patient Relations. Being a teenager in a hospital doesn't mean you lose your agency.

instruction: The nurses keep checking on me at night and waking me up. Who told them to do that?
response: Night-time checks are a standard part of nursing care ordered by your physician and carried out by the nursing team. They're there to ensure your safety, comfort, and to catch any changes in your condition early. The frequency of checks depends on your medical situation — some patients require more frequent monitoring than others. I know interrupted sleep is frustrating, especially when you're trying to recover. If it's really affecting your rest, it's worth mentioning to your nurse or doctor to see if there's any flexibility, but safety always comes first.

instruction: Are there any support resources specifically for my siblings?
response: Yes — Children's Hospital recognizes that a sibling's hospitalization affects the whole family. Child Life Specialists work with siblings as well as patients, and the Heroes' Circle program is available to siblings too, teaching breathing, relaxation, and coping techniques. Social workers can support your family as a unit, and spaces like the School-Age Activity Room and Ashley's Backyard are available to visiting siblings. If your brother or sister is struggling, your care team can help connect them with age-appropriate support.

instruction: Can anyone explain the Comfort Promise to me in a way that's not patronizing?
response: Sure. The Comfort Promise is an evidence-based commitment to reduce pain and anxiety during needle procedures. Here's what it involves: topical anesthetic to numb the site, comfort positioning (supportive positions rather than being held down, which research shows has significant negative effects), and distraction techniques. The clinical rationale is solid — untreated procedural pain is linked to increased pain sensitivity in future procedures, health-care avoidance, slower recovery, and vaccine hesitancy. You're encouraged to actively participate in choosing which strategies work for you. You can ask for any or all of them before any needle procedure. It's not about coddling — it's about evidence-based pain management.

instruction: Who's responsible for the after-hours entrance?
response: Security controls the after-hours entrance. The B Tower main entrance is open from 6 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. daily. After 8:30 p.m., access is controlled by security — caregivers need to check in with the guard for permission to enter. The parking garage entrance is technically open 24 hours, but after hours you'll still need to check in with security. Zone D entrances on Levels 2 and 3 are locked from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m., and Zone D Level 4 and Zone B Level 8 are locked 24/7. If you need to contact security, dispatch is at extension 52281.

instruction: My family uses traditional tobacco for cultural purposes. Does anyone here accommodate that?
response: Yes. Under the Smoke-Free Ontario Act, there's an exemption for traditional use of tobacco by Indigenous peoples. LHSC provides a designated space for Indigenous peoples to use tobacco for traditional, cultural, or spiritual purposes. The Youth Indigenous Wellness Consultant can also support cultural practices during your stay. If you'd like to access this space or connect with Indigenous Health services, ask your care team or email IndigenousHealth@lhsc.on.ca. The hospital is committed to respecting cultural and spiritual practices.

instruction: Is there Wi-Fi here and who do I contact if it's not working?
response: Yes — the hospital has Wi-Fi for patients. There's also a patient entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free and access your own streaming accounts. If you're having trouble connecting, the Data Valet/Wi-Fi support line is 1-800-642-3958. You can also use your own cell phone to make calls and stay connected with friends and family. Patient telephones are available too for local and toll-free calls at no cost.

instruction: Someone said there's a SMILE Room. What's that about?
response: The SMILE Room is in room B6-261 on the sixth floor. It's a sensory room filled with equipment designed for relaxation or stimulation — bubble columns, fibre optics, mirrors, music, and more. It can be used by patients who need a sensory break, whether that's calming down or being gently stimulated. A Child Life Specialist or your nurse can help you access it. It's one of those resources that might sound unusual but is actually well-grounded in therapeutic approaches to sensory regulation.

instruction: Why do I need to wear slip-proof socks?
response: Your nurse provided those as part of falls prevention. Hospital floors can be slippery, and when you're recovering from illness, injury, or a procedure, your balance and strength might not be what they usually are. Slip-proof socks, slippers, or shoes reduce your risk of a fall. Your nurse does a formal falls assessment and will discuss other prevention steps with you, like keeping bed rails up and asking for help before getting out of bed. It might seem minor, but falls in hospitals can cause real setbacks in your recovery.

instruction: I got a red bracelet in addition to my regular one. Why?
response: The red bracelet is an allergy alert bracelet. It's placed on patients who have known allergies — whether to medications, foods, or environmental factors — so that every member of your care team is immediately aware. It serves as a visual, always-present reminder alongside the allergy information in your chart. Your nurse will have documented your allergies when you were admitted, and the red bracelet ensures that even someone seeing you for the first time — like a new nurse or technician — knows to check before administering anything.

instruction: I overheard someone mention ethics consultation. When would that happen?
response: LHSC has a clinical ethics consultation service available when patients, families, or health-care providers are facing a difficult ethical decision in a care situation. This could involve choices about treatment options, end-of-life care, consent, or other complex situations where there isn't one clear right answer. The ethicist is trained to help all parties identify, clarify, and work through ethical concerns. Any patient, family member, or care provider can request an ethics consultation. It's not adversarial — it's a structured way to navigate genuinely hard decisions together.

instruction: Someone mentioned an Ontario Health atHome referral. Does that mean I'm going home soon?
response: Not necessarily in the immediate sense, but it does mean your care team is starting to think about your discharge plan — which actually begins early in your hospital stay. An Ontario Health atHome Care Coordinator assesses what equipment or services you might need at home. If your stay is longer than 14 days, a new referral is required. The coordinator at extension 52249 helps arrange things like home nursing, therapy services, or medical equipment. It's a standard part of discharge planning, and it's a good sign that your care team is proactively preparing for your transition home.

instruction: What's the deal with the Paediatric Medical Day Unit?
response: The Paediatric Medical Day Unit (PMDU) is where children and teens receive treatments that don't require an overnight stay — things like infusions, transfusions, or other medical procedures that can be completed in a single day. The team there includes nurses and other health-care professionals who specialize in outpatient paediatric care. They provide light snacks for patients receiving treatment. The PMDU can be reached at extension 58434 if your family has questions.

instruction: Can I talk to someone about the cost of my care?
response: The Business Office at Victoria Hospital, located in Zone D, third floor, room D3-400, handles billing questions. While most care is covered by OHIP, there may be charges for certain supplies or devices — crutches, surgical supplies, breast pumps, and similar items. You'll receive an invoice by mail, and payment can be made at the bank, by cheque, or online by credit card with a small convenience fee. A social worker can also help if your family is facing financial strain — they're trained to connect families with financial resources and community support programs.

instruction: What does the hospital operator do?
response: The hospital operator is the person who answers the main LHSC phone line at 519-685-8500 when you press 0. They route incoming calls to the correct department, unit, or staff member. If someone outside the hospital wants to reach you, they'll likely go through the operator first. The operator can connect callers to pretty much any department — from your inpatient unit to Patient Relations to the parking office. It's the central switchboard for the entire hospital.

instruction: There's someone in the lounge who said they volunteer here. Why do people volunteer at a hospital?
response: People volunteer at Children's Hospital for a range of reasons — some are students gaining health-care experience, others are community members who want to give back, and some are former patients or family members who want to support others going through what they went through. Volunteers help at information desks, guide stations, playrooms, and special events. They're at the B1 entrance and B2 lobby on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. They're not part of your medical team, but they contribute to the overall experience by providing guidance, companionship, and support. It takes real commitment to volunteer your time in a hospital setting.

instruction: Who's the person who scanned my armband barcode before drawing blood?
response: That was either a nurse, a phlebotomist (a technician trained specifically in blood draws), or a lab technician. The barcode scan is a safety check — it verifies your identity against the lab order to ensure the right blood work is being done on the right patient. Your armband contains your name, date of birth, and hospital ID number encoded in that barcode. It's a quick step, but it's a critical layer of error prevention in the hospital's patient safety protocol.

instruction: What happens if I feel unsafe or uncomfortable with someone on my care team?
response: You have every right to speak up. Start by telling your parent or caregiver, and then communicate your concern to your nurse or another trusted member of your care team. If the situation isn't resolved, the Patient Relations Office is your next escalation point — extension 52036 or patientrelations@lhsc.on.ca. You can also ask to speak with a social worker. LHSC is committed to safe, respectful care. Advocating for yourself when something doesn't feel right is not only okay — it's exactly what the hospital encourages.

instruction: Is the person taking X-rays the same as my doctor?
response: No — that's typically a medical imaging technologist or radiologic technologist. They're specifically trained to operate diagnostic imaging equipment like X-ray machines, CT scanners, and other imaging technology. They capture the images, which are then reviewed and interpreted by a radiologist (a physician who specializes in reading medical images). Your attending physician receives the results and incorporates them into your care plan. The technologist is focused on getting clear, accurate images while keeping your radiation exposure as low as possible.

instruction: Can my family ask for a different room?
response: Your family can request a specific room type, but the hospital makes assignments based on availability and infection-control requirements. Insurance-related requests may also not always be possible to accommodate. If you have a specific concern — like needing more space for medical equipment, privacy issues, or infection control — communicate that to your nurse or care team and they'll do what they can. Room assignments aren't arbitrary, but the hospital does try to meet family preferences where feasible.

instruction: What does the Car Seat Technician do?
response: The Car Seat Technicians at LHSC's Trauma Program offer one-on-one consultations — both virtually and in person — to make sure car seats are installed correctly. By law, all children must travel in an approved car seat, so this is especially important when you're being discharged. If your child has specific mobility or medical needs post-discharge, a physiotherapist or occupational therapist may also help explore safe transportation options. Your nurse can help schedule a car seat consultation before you leave.

instruction: Is there anyone who can help me figure out my feelings about a chronic diagnosis?
response: There are several people on your team who can help. Paediatric psychologists specialize in helping children and teens adjust to illness and develop coping strategies for managing physical, emotional, and behavioural symptoms. Social workers provide emotional support and can connect you with community resources. Child Life Specialists can help you process your feelings through conversation, activities, or creative expression. Spiritual Care Specialists are also available regardless of your religious background. You're not expected to handle a chronic diagnosis on your own — ask your nurse for a referral to whichever service feels like the right fit.

instruction: Why are there so many people on my care team? It's overwhelming.
response: That's a really valid feeling. The number of people involved in your care reflects the complexity of paediatric medicine and the hospital's commitment to treating you holistically — not just the medical issue, but your nutrition, mobility, mental health, family dynamics, and comfort. At Children's Hospital, your team might include a physician, residents, nurses, nurse practitioners, a pharmacist, dietitian, physiotherapist, occupational therapist, speech therapist, social worker, Child Life Specialist, and others depending on your needs. Not all of them will be actively involved at all times. If it feels overwhelming, ask your primary nurse to help you understand who's doing what — they're your best point of contact for navigating the team.

instruction: Who manages the locked unit on B6?
response: The B6 inpatient unit is managed by the nursing and clinical team assigned to that floor. It's a locked unit, meaning the doors require a confidential code to enter and exit. When you're admitted, your nurse provides the code to your family. The locked setup is a safety measure to protect the patients on the unit. If you have questions about the unit's policies or need to contact staff directly, B6-100 can be reached at extension 52060 and B6-200 at extension 58196.

instruction: Can I request to talk to a pharmacist about my meds directly?
response: Yes, absolutely. At Children's Hospital, a pharmacist is available to come to your room and answer your questions or address concerns about your medications. Just ask your nurse to arrange it. Pharmacists can explain what each medication does, how to take it, potential side effects, and drug interactions. If you're on several medications, they can also prepare a medication calendar for you and your family before discharge. Being informed about what you're taking is a reasonable and important expectation.

instruction: I noticed some staff wearing different coloured scrubs. Does the colour mean something?
response: In many hospitals, scrub colours can indicate different departments or roles — for example, surgical staff might wear one colour while nurses wear another. The specifics vary between hospitals, and LHSC doesn't have a universally standardized colour-coding system that's been published for patients. If you're curious about what a particular person's role is, the most reliable approach is to check their name badge, which should display their name and title. You can also just ask — staff expect that question and are happy to introduce themselves.

instruction: Someone talked to my family about bereavement support. Who was that?
response: That was likely a Spiritual Care Specialist or a social worker. Bereavement care at LHSC is provided by both of those services. The hospital also holds an annual 'Remembering the Children' memorial event each fall — a non-religious event that acknowledges all infants and children who have passed away at LHSC over the year. Your nurse can provide a 'Consent to be Contacted' form if your family is interested in attending. These services exist to provide compassionate support during an incredibly difficult time.

instruction: Who can walk me through what's going to happen during my procedure?
response: A Child Life Specialist is specifically trained to prepare patients for procedures — they'll explain what will happen step by step, describe what you might see, hear, and feel, and help you develop a coping plan. Your nurse and physician can also walk you through the clinical details. For surgical procedures, the PPI program may offer a tour of Day Surgery and the Operating Room. You're entitled to understand what's happening to your body before it happens. Don't hesitate to ask for as much information as you need.

instruction: I'm being discharged soon. Who all is involved in that process?
response: Discharge planning at Children's Hospital is a team effort that starts early in your stay. Your physician determines when you're medically ready. Your nurse reviews medications, care instructions, and follow-up appointments with your family. A pharmacist may prepare a medication calendar. If you need home care services or equipment, an Ontario Health atHome Care Coordinator assesses your needs. A social worker may help with financial resources, school re-entry, or community services. A physiotherapist or occupational therapist may advise on mobility and safe transportation. Your family is responsible for arranging your ride home — your nurse can provide a brochure about transport options if needed. The goal is for you to leave with a clear plan and no unanswered questions.

instruction: What's the Great Moments Recognition Program?
response: It's LHSC's way of recognizing staff, physicians, volunteers, learners, and patient partners who go above and beyond. If someone on your care team made a real difference in your experience, you or your family can fill out a short form on the LHSC website. The person you recognize receives a letter of appreciation from an LHSC supervisor and a small item of recognition, supported by London Health Sciences Foundation and Children's Health Foundation. You don't even need to remember their exact name — if you describe the details of the interaction, the program can help identify who it was.

instruction: Is there someone who can help me advocate for my own care?
response: Several people can support you in that. Your primary nurse is your daily advocate and point of contact. Social workers specialize in advocacy and can help you communicate with your care team, navigate decisions, and prepare for discharge. The Shared Decision Making program provides Decision Coaches who ensure your values are part of the decision-making process. Patient Relations is available if you feel your voice isn't being heard. And honestly, you're already advocating for yourself by asking this question. Children's Hospital explicitly encourages patients and families to be active partners in care.

instruction: Who are the people at the nurses' station?
response: The nurses' station is the operational hub of your unit. You'll typically see your assigned nurses, the charge nurse (the nurse overseeing the unit for that shift), the unit clerk (who handles administrative tasks like phones and paperwork), and sometimes residents, nurse practitioners, or physicians reviewing charts or making calls. Other team members — dietitians, pharmacists, therapists — may stop by to discuss patient care. It's a busy area, but the people there are your front line for questions, requests, and updates.

instruction: What's the B6 inpatient unit like and who works there?
response: The B6 inpatient unit houses paediatric patients on the sixth floor of Zone B. It's a locked unit — your family gets a confidential code upon admission. The team includes nurses (RNs and RPNs), physicians, residents, Child Life Specialists, social workers, and other allied health professionals. There are two sections — B6-100 and B6-200 — each with their own contact number. The unit has pantries in B6-149 and B6-231 with drinks and light snacks, a family fridge, the Culliton Family Lounge in B6-110, Ashley's Backyard playroom in B6-259, quiet rooms, the SMILE Room in B6-261, and the School-Age Activity Room in B6-065. One overnight sleep space is provided for a family member.

instruction: I don't want a student examining me. Do I have the right to refuse?
response: Yes, you have the right to decline having a medical student involved in your care or examination. Children's Hospital is a teaching hospital, and medical students participate in care under supervision as part of their training, but your consent matters. If you're uncomfortable, communicate this to your nurse or attending physician. Your care will not be affected by your decision. It's your body and your care experience — having the confidence to set that boundary is completely reasonable.

instruction: Someone asked me about research participation. Is that safe?
response: Clinical research at LHSC must be reviewed and approved by the London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute and a qualified Research Ethics Board before any patient is ever approached. These boards exist to protect participants. You should receive a detailed Letter of Information explaining the study's purpose, procedures, risks, and your rights. Participation is always completely voluntary — declining has zero effect on your care. Take your time, read everything, and ask as many questions as you need. If you have concerns about a study, you can contact LHSCRI's Quality Assurance and Education Team or the Patient Relations Office. Being cautious about research participation is not just okay — it's expected.

instruction: Why would my nurse ask me questions when my parents aren't in the room?
response: It's standard practice for health-care providers to have some one-on-one time with adolescent patients. This gives you a safe space to ask questions, share concerns, or discuss things you might not feel comfortable bringing up in front of your parents. It could be about your health, your emotional state, or anything else. It's not about excluding your parents — it's about respecting your developing autonomy and giving you room to be honest. Whatever you discuss is treated with appropriate confidentiality.

instruction: What's the emergency response team?
response: The emergency response team, sometimes called a code team or rapid response team, is a group of highly trained health-care professionals who respond to medical emergencies within the hospital. If a patient's condition deteriorates rapidly, staff can activate the emergency response using extension 55555. The team typically includes physicians, nurses, and respiratory therapists who arrive quickly to stabilize the patient. You might hear overhead announcements or see rapid movement in the halls — that's the system working as designed. Security dispatch at extension 52281 handles non-medical emergencies.

instruction: Can my friend visit me? Who decides?
response: Visiting at Children's Hospital is based on the patient's condition, care needs, and wishes, as well as unit-specific guidelines. It's best to check with your unit staff about optimal visiting times. Visiting may be restricted for infection control, patient safety, or privacy reasons. After 8 p.m., visitors are asked to remain in the patient's room and let unit staff know when they arrive or leave. Everyone visiting should wash their hands and shouldn't come if they're sick or have been unwell in the past week. Talk to your nurse about the visiting guidelines for your specific unit — they can help you figure out the best time for your friend to come.

instruction: Who manages infection control on my unit and what are the precautions about?
response: Infection prevention and control is managed hospital-wide by LHSC's Infection Prevention and Control team, with protocols carried out by every member of your care team. If extra precautions are needed — for example, if you have an infectious condition — a sign will be posted at your room entry. Visitors should stop at the nurses' station for instructions before entering. Precautions might include wearing gloves, a gown, a mask, or eye protection. You may be asked to stay in your room and keep personal items minimal to facilitate cleaning. Alcohol-based hand rub is the preferred method for hand hygiene and is available throughout the unit. These measures protect you, other patients, and staff.

instruction: What's the role of the respiratory therapist?
response: A respiratory therapist, or RT, specializes in your lungs and breathing. At Children's Hospital, RTs manage ventilators and breathing equipment, perform breathing tests like spirometry, administer inhaled medications, and help with airway management. In critical care settings like the PCCU, they work closely with the medical team to support patients who need mechanical ventilation. If you're having breathing difficulties or have a respiratory condition, an RT is a key member of your care team. They can explain what the equipment does and answer questions about your respiratory treatment plan.

instruction: Can I bring my own food? Who do I check with?
response: You should always check with your care team before eating anything that wasn't provided by the hospital. There may be medical reasons — like upcoming tests, procedures, or a prescribed diet — that restrict what you can eat. If your care team approves outside food, the B6 inpatient unit has a family refrigerator with a freezer for personal food storage in the pantries at B6-149 and B6-231. Label and date your items. The PCCU has a small fridge in the waiting room. The closest retail food option is On the Go featuring Tim Hortons on the second floor of Zone B, open weekdays 6:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vending machines are on the first and third floors of Zone B near the elevators.

instruction: What does my nurse actually do all day?
response: Your nurse is the backbone of your daily care. They administer medications, monitor your vital signs, assess your condition, manage IVs and other equipment, coordinate tests and appointments, communicate with your physicians and the rest of your care team, document everything in your chart, provide patient education, and respond to your needs and concerns throughout their shift. They also participate in bedside shift change reports twice a day and perform regular safety checks — including overnight. Nurses at Children's Hospital work closely with families, organize discharge follow-ups, and serve as your primary point of contact for navigating the hospital system.

instruction: Is there anyone who can help with school work while I'm here?
response: The Transitions in Care team and social workers can help coordinate with your school about missed work and re-entry plans. Child Life Specialists may also help facilitate educational activities. If you're on the B6 unit, the School-Age Activity Room in B6-065 has structured activities available. For formal school support — like having assignments sent to the hospital or arranging accommodations for your return — your social worker can communicate directly with your school administration. Bring this up with your care team early in your stay so arrangements can be made before you're discharged.

instruction: Someone mentioned a 'charge nurse.' What's that?
response: The charge nurse is the nurse who oversees the entire unit for a given shift. They manage patient assignments, coordinate admissions and discharges, handle staffing issues, and serve as a resource for other nurses. If you have a concern that your assigned nurse can't resolve, or if you want to discuss something at a unit-management level — like a room issue or care concern — the charge nurse is a good person to ask for. They're typically based at or near the nurses' station and have a broader view of what's happening across the whole unit.

instruction: What do I need to know about the people in the Emergency Department?
response: The Paediatric Emergency Department team includes emergency physicians, nurses, triage nurses (who assess how urgently you need care), and potentially specialists called in for specific issues. You'll pass through a weapons detection system at the entrance staffed by security. A triage nurse will evaluate your symptoms and assign a priority level. One caregiver is expected to stay with you at all times. There are no sleeping accommodations in the ED, but staff will try to provide a reclining chair, pillows, and blankets. The ED can be reached at extension 58141. Wait times vary based on severity — patients with the most urgent needs are seen first, not necessarily in arrival order.

instruction: Who handles my medications when I'm admitted and is it different from home?
response: When you're admitted, your care team does a medication reconciliation — they review everything you're currently taking, including prescriptions, over-the-counter products, herbal supplements, vitamins, creams, inhalers, and eye drops. Medications from home shouldn't be taken unless approved by your care team, because the hospital will supply what's been prescribed and approved for use at LHSC. Your nurse administers your medications during your stay, scanning your armband each time. Before discharge, you'll receive an updated medication list to share with your family doctor and pharmacy. A pharmacist can come to your room to answer any questions about changes to your medications.

instruction: Is there someone I can talk to about end-of-life stuff?
response: Yes — and it takes courage to ask that question. The Paediatric Symptom Management and Supportive Care Services (PSMSC) team specializes in caring for children and teens with serious illnesses, including those approaching end of life. Their focus is on quality of life and easing pain and suffering. Spiritual Care Specialists are also available for emotional and existential support regardless of your faith background. Social workers can help with family communication and planning. Psychologists offer therapeutic support for processing what you're going through. You can ask your care team to connect you with any or all of these services. You don't have to navigate this alone.

instruction: That person who just came in... who were they again?
response: It's hard to keep track of everyone in a busy hospital! If you didn't catch who someone was, you can always ask the next time they come in: 'Can you tell me your name and what you do here?' Everyone who works here wears a badge with their name and role, so a quick look at that helps too. There's no embarrassing way to ask — the team knows they're meeting lots of new patients and they expect you to not remember everyone.

instruction: How come I have so many different doctors if I'm just one person?
response: It might feel like a lot, but each of those doctors is an expert in a different part of how your body works. Your main doctor looks at the whole picture, and specialists focus on specific things — like if one doctor knows everything about hearts and another knows everything about lungs. Having a team means more people checking that everything is okay from different angles. It's actually a sign that your hospital is taking good care of you. Your nurse can introduce you to the main members of your team if all the names and faces are getting blurry.

instruction: I feel like the only thing that helped was the nurse from last night but I don't even know her name.
response: That's worth following up on. Ask your nurse today to look up who was on last night — nurses' schedules are tracked and the charge nurse should be able to tell you. Once you know the name, you can ask for that person to be assigned to you when they're working and let them know they made a difference. Feeling connected to a specific person on the team is genuinely valuable and your care team should take that seriously.

instruction: I don't understand why I need to see a physio if I'm not injured.
response: Physiotherapy isn't only for injuries — it's for anyone whose body needs support getting back to full movement and function. After being in bed for even a few days, muscles can get weaker and joints stiffer than you'd expect. A physio can help you regain strength safely, make sure you're moving correctly while you're healing, and give you exercises that support your recovery. It's not a sign that something extra is wrong — it's part of the plan to help you get back to normal as completely as possible.

instruction: I haven't seen my doctor today. Is that bad?
response: Not necessarily — it depends on where you are in your care. On some days, especially if things are going as expected, your doctor may visit briefly or review your chart without coming into your room. It doesn't mean they've forgotten about you. If you feel like you haven't gotten an update and want one, ask your nurse: 'Has the doctor reviewed my chart today? Is there anything new?' Your nurse can get you that information or arrange for the doctor to stop in. You always have the right to know what's going on with your care.
